abstract: Nuclear read-outs on an organ-on-a-chip (cell number, proliferation, viability) start from a nuclear stain, but fixation ends the experiment, live DNA dyes add phototoxic exposure, and reporter lines are impractical for primary or iPSC-derived tissue. In-silico labeling (ISL) predicts the stain from bright-field, but a point prediction gives no warning when it is wrong. ChipStain predicts the H2B nuclear channel from one bright-field image together with a per-pixel uncertainty σ (U-Net with an ImageNet ResNet-34 encoder, β-NLL heteroscedastic head, 8× test-time augmentation). We validate the uncertainty, not only the image, on a public HeLa time-lapse in a 96-well plate (held-out well, 125 images, 3 training seeds; no chip data were available to us). Against the same U-Net with TTA, ChipStain matches the correlation with the real stain (r {{n_full_pearson}} vs {{n_bt_pearson}}) at a small, consistent pixel-fidelity cost (MAE +{{n_mae_rel}} %). Its σ ranks pixel errors better (Spearman ρ {{n_full_rho}} vs {{n_bt_rho}}; AUSE {{n_full_ause}} vs {{n_bt_ause}}; in every seed) and is approximately calibrated (nominal 95 % intervals cover {{n_cal_95}} % of pixels). Under simulated blur and a phase-contrast input every model's prediction fails; whether σ warns is seed-dependent for all models (ChipStain: in {{n_shift_cs_defocus_seeds_ok}} seeds — the released one), so σ is not a reliable drift alarm, whereas added noise is flagged by every model in every seed. A σ gate fixed on validation data cuts the error of label-free doubling times from {{n_pl_cs_bias_all}} % to {{n_pl_cs_bias_gate}} %. {{neural_summary}}For nuclei counting alone, a direct bright-field segmenter is more accurate (Cellpose F1 {{n_cp_f1}} vs {{n_full_segf1}}); ChipStain's value is a fluorescence-like image plus a calibrated trust signal. Open code and weights; CPU inference.
neural_abstract: On human iPSC-derived motor neurons, fine-tuning on a single well raises Pearson r from {{n_nz_cs_r}} (zero-shot) to {{n_nf_cs_k1_r}}.

calibration_text: ChipStain + TTA is close to calibrated without any correction: the nominal 68.3 % and 95 % intervals cover {{n_cal_68}} % and {{n_cal_95}} % of test pixels, and the scale factor fitted on the validation split is {{n_cal_scale}}. Coverage is pooled over pixels, most of which are background; restricted to pixels inside the reference nuclei, the 95 % interval covers {{n_cal_fg95}} %. The TTA disagreement of the L1 U-Nets is far too small to be read as a standard deviation (the U-Net's 68.3 % interval covers {{n_cal_unet_68}} %; it needs scaling by ×{{n_cal_unet_scale}}): it can rank errors but not quantify them. Calibration holds in distribution only: under imaging shift (§6.7) σ does not track the much larger error in most training runs.
shift_text: All models' predictions degrade under blur and the modality swap (Figure 6A); ChipStain's degrades at least as much as the L1 models' (Pearson r under 1 px blur {{n_shift_cs_r_def1}} vs {{n_shift_bu_r_def1}} for the U-Net; with phase contrast {{n_shift_cs_r_dpc}} vs {{n_shift_bu_r_dpc}}): its mean prediction is not more robust. Whether the uncertainty notices is, for every model, a property of the individual training run rather than of the method. With three seeds per model, mean σ separates blurred from clean images (AUROC > 0.8) in {{n_shift_cs_defocus_seeds_ok}} ChipStain seeds, {{n_shift_bu_defocus_seeds_ok}} U-Net seeds and {{n_shift_pre_defocus_seeds_ok}} ImageNet-L1 seeds, and falls under blur (AUROC < 0.2, a silent failure) in {{n_shift_cs_defocus_seeds_down}}, {{n_shift_bu_defocus_seeds_down}} and {{n_shift_pre_defocus_seeds_down}} seeds respectively; for the phase-contrast input the counts are {{n_shift_cs_dpc_seeds_ok}}, {{n_shift_bu_dpc_seeds_ok}} and {{n_shift_pre_dpc_seeds_ok}} (Table 7). The released seed-0 ChipStain checkpoint is one of the runs whose σ does rise (×{{n_shift_cs_s0_def4x}} under 4 px blur, ×{{n_shift_cs_s0_dpcx}} with phase contrast), which is what the demo shows — but the other two ChipStain seeds become less uncertain. Pooling clean and shifted images, σ separates failed (r < 0.5) from successful (r > 0.7) predictions only weakly (AUROC {{n_shift_cs_sig_fail}} ChipStain, {{n_shift_bu_sig_fail}} U-Net, {{n_shift_pre_sig_fail}} ImageNet-L1; large seed spread). Additive noise of 10–20 % is flagged by every model in every seed. Affine contrast changes were not tested: the per-image normalisation cancels them exactly. Conclusion: in-distribution, ChipStain's σ ranks errors well and is calibrated (§6.5); out of distribution, neither its σ nor TTA disagreement is a dependable drift alarm, and a deployment must check new imaging conditions with paired images.
ensemble_text: Combining the three training seeds, a deep ensemble of plain U-Nets yields a poor uncertainty (ρ {{n_ens_bu_rho}}, AUSE {{n_ens_bu_ause}}): with three members, the disagreement of point predictors is too noisy to rank errors. An ensemble of ImageNet-initialised L1 U-Nets does better (ρ {{n_ens_pre_rho}}, AUSE {{n_ens_pre_ause}}) but still trails a single ChipStain model with TTA. A ChipStain ensemble without TTA gives the best ranking of any configuration (ρ {{n_ens_cs_rho}}, AUSE {{n_ens_cs_ause}}), and with TTA it reaches Pearson r {{n_ens_cstta_pearson}} and seg-F1 {{n_ens_cstta_segf1}}, absorbing single-seed failures. Three models triple the cost, so the single TTA model is the released default.
counting_text: Counting nuclei on the prediction with a fixed, simple watershed reaches F1 {{n_full_segf1}} (ChipStain + TTA) against the StarDist reference; the same watershed on the real stain reaches {{n_real_segf1}}, so much of the gap to perfect agreement is the segmenter (Appendix A). Count agreement is better than object agreement because merges and splits partly cancel. A biologist will ask whether one should predict the stain at all if the goal is a count. The dataset author's Cellpose model, trained on this dataset's training split to segment nuclei directly from bright-field (and quality-controlled by its author on this held-out well), reaches F1 {{n_cp_f1}} on the same test images with a mean count error of {{n_cp_count_err}} % (Table 8) — better than counting on our prediction, and better than our watershed on the real stain, because it was trained to reproduce exactly the StarDist label definition used as reference. For counting alone, direct segmentation is the better tool. {{cellpose_pred_text}}ISL earns its place differently: it returns an intensity image that any downstream pipeline can use (intensity, texture, chromatin condensation, morphology — not only outlines), and a calibrated uncertainty. {{cellpose_shift_text}}We also tested whether ChipStain's mean σ predicts where Cellpose fails in distribution; it does not (ρ = {{n_cp_sigma_rho}}), so we make no claim that the two are complementary there.
nucleus_text: At the level of single nuclei, σ is weak. The mean σ inside a predicted nucleus flags detections that match no reference nucleus with AUROC {{n_nuc_cs}} — slightly below a trivial 'dim nucleus' score on the same predictions ({{n_nuc_dim_cs}}) — and the U-Net's TTA disagreement does better on its own predictions ({{n_nuc_bt}}); the 3-seed ensemble does not help ({{n_nuc_ens}}). Discarding uncertain detections raises precision but lowers recall and F1 for every score (Figure 7). We therefore use per-nucleus σ only as a visual review aid and claim no advantage at this level.
prolif_text: Label-free counts reproduce the reference doubling time ({{n_pl_ref_dt}} h) with a mean absolute bias of {{n_pl_cs_bias_all}} % over the three ChipStain seeds ({{n_pl_bt_bias_all}} % for U-Net + TTA). The errors are driven by failed frames: one ChipStain seed collapses on two fields (worst seed {{n_pl_cs_worst_all}} %), and those catastrophic frames are that seed's three highest-σ test images. The σ gate, fixed on validation data with a 5 % false-alarm budget, drops flagged frames before fitting: the mean bias falls to {{n_pl_cs_bias_gate}} % (worst seed {{n_pl_cs_worst_gate}} %) and the mean absolute per-field error from {{n_pl_cs_mape_all}} % to {{n_pl_cs_mape_gate}} %. The same gate on the U-Net's TTA disagreement also helps ({{n_pl_bt_bias_all}} % → {{n_pl_bt_bias_gate}} %), so the gate is not specific to ChipStain; it leaves the U-Net's failing seed at {{n_pl_bt_worst_gate}} %. Over all seeds the ChipStain gate flags {{n_pl_cs_flagged}} of {{n_pl_frames_total}} test frames — more than the 5 % validation budget, because the test well differs slightly from the validation fields — and catches {{n_pl_cs_caught}} of the frames whose detection failed (F1 < 0.5): it catches catastrophic failures, not moderate ones. Fields left with fewer than three frames ({{n_pl_cs_review}} field-runs) are routed to review instead of being reported.
timelapse_text: On the full recording of one held-out field ({{n_tl_frames}} frames over 60 h, Figures 9–10) the label-free counts follow the real-stain counts with a mean error of {{n_tl_count_err}} % and give a doubling time of {{n_tl_dt_pred}} h versus {{n_tl_dt_real}} h, both counted with the same watershed — a growth curve from bright-field alone, without a single fluorescence exposure. Object-level agreement between the two segmentations is modest (median F1 {{n_tl_f1}}) because both use the simple watershed. Mean σ rises as the field becomes crowded and tracks per-frame failure (ρ(mean σ, 1 − F1) = {{n_tl_rho}}), which is confounded by density and time; frames after ≈37 h are beyond the densest training time-point. Five of the 240 frames are also test images; the other 235 were never used.
ablation_text: Table 3 changes one factor at a time (3 seeds each, no TTA). The single-factor effects that are robust — CI excluding zero, no seed going the other way, at least two seeds significant — are: {{n_abl_robust}}. Effects not listed are within run-to-run variation. In particular the fidelity cost of ChipStain should be read through the two steps L1 → MSE and MSE → β-NLL, which separate the loss family from the variance head.
neural_text: We applied the HeLa models to human iPSC-derived motor-neuron cultures (Christiansen et al. 2018, Condition A; 22 training and 3 test wells, bright-field z-stacks and widefield DAPI) — neurons in a dish, not an OoC. The rescale factor ({{n_neural_scale}}) and the bright-field z-plane ({{n_neural_z}}) were chosen on two validation wells with the ChipStain checkpoint and agree with an independent nucleus-size estimate. Zero-shot, ChipStain reaches Pearson r {{n_nz_cs_r}} with the real DAPI (U-Net {{n_nz_bu_r}}), but counting on the prediction is poor (F1 against the real-DAPI segmentation {{n_nz_cs_f1}}; count {{n_nz_cs_count}} %), and its mean σ ({{n_nz_cs_sigma}}) stays inside the HeLa test range ({{n_sigma_range}}): the uncertainty does not signal that the model is out of domain — consistent with §6.7. Fine-tuning from the HeLa weights with a single training well raises r to {{n_nf_cs_k1_r}} (F1 {{n_nf_cs_k1_f1}}), and with {{n_nf_kmax}} wells to {{n_nf_cs_k20_r}} (F1 {{n_nf_cs_k20_f1}}); starting from ImageNet instead gives {{n_nf_in_k1_r}} and {{n_nf_in_k20_r}}. These fine-tuning runs use one seed and the first k wells, so small differences are not meaningful; the experiment shows that a small paired set adapts the model to a new cell type and imaging system.
sec_limitations:
• No organ-on-a-chip data; one plate, one session. All validation uses 2-D cells in a well plate (HeLa) or a dish (neurons). The three HeLa wells come from one plate and one imaging session, so the hold-out measures well-to-well generalisation only. The shift test approximates some chip optics, not 3-D tissue, flow or PDMS autofluorescence. Before use on a chip, fine-tune on paired images from that device and re-check Tables 1, 5 and 7.
  • Fidelity cost. Against the same U-Net with TTA, ChipStain has equal correlation but {{n_mae_rel}} % higher MAE and lower SSIM.
  • Robustness and drift. Under blur and modality change ChipStain's prediction degrades at least as much as the L1 models'. Whether σ then rises is seed-dependent for every model ({{n_shift_cs_defocus_seeds_ok}} ChipStain seeds); σ is not a dependable drift alarm.
  • Scope of the uncertainty. σ ranks pixel errors well and is near-calibrated in distribution, but at a single 20 % cut-off it is only slightly better than ranking by predicted intensity; at the nucleus level it is no better than a dim-nucleus heuristic; in distribution its frame-level signal is matched by the U-Net's TTA disagreement and largely reflects cell density; and the frame gate catches catastrophic, not moderate, failures.
  • Counting. A direct bright-field segmenter trained on matching labels counts nuclei better than counting on our prediction (§6.8).
  • Automatic references. F1 and counts are measured against StarDist labels on the real stain, not manual annotation; our watershed on the real stain reaches F1 {{n_real_segf1}} — a reference level, not a bound.
  • Training variability. One of three ChipStain seeds fails on two test fields (σ flags them); one U-Net seed loses {{n_bu_seed_gap}} nuclei F1. Retraining lands within the seed spread of Table 1, not on identical numbers; hence three seeds and seed-aware statistics throughout.
  • Target. mCherry-H2B is a genetically encoded reporter; on this dataset no dye is actually avoided. The value applies where such a reporter is unavailable.
  • Ethics. No human-subject, clinical or personal data. The main risk is over-trusting a hallucinated prediction, which σ and the gate are designed to reduce but cannot eliminate.
sec_impact:
Where ChipStain could help. Once fine-tuned on a small paired set from the target device, it could provide a quality-controlled, label-free nuclear channel for long recordings: growth and viability curves without fixation or repeated dye exposure, a freed fluorescence channel for a functional reporter, and a σ gate that keeps catastrophic frames out of the analysis (§6.10; the only proliferation evidence so far is from a well plate). Its mean σ should not be relied on as an imaging-drift alarm: under blur or a change of modality it rises only in some training runs (§6.7), so new imaging conditions must be checked with paired images. For pure nuclear counting a direct segmenter should be preferred (§6.8).

Neural OoC (the supporting organisation's focus). Neurons are post-mitotic, so label-free nuclear counts and nuclear condensation over weeks are a natural viability/neurotoxicity end-point; repeated live DNA dyes perturb such cultures, and reporter lines are rarely available for iPSC-derived neurons. §6.11 tests transfer to human iPSC-derived motor neurons.

Path to a chip. (1) Acquire a small set of paired bright-field / nuclear-stain images on the target device (we did not measure how many are needed on a chip; §6.11 measures it for neurons in a dish); (2) fine-tune from the released weights; (3) recalibrate σ with one scalar on held-out pairs; (4) set the frame gate on validation frames; (5) monitor mean σ in production as one signal among others, re-checking with paired images whenever the imaging changes. Inference runs on a CPU and depends on nothing proprietary. A trustworthy label-free nuclear channel is a prerequisite for the organisers' goal of AI-driven OoC digital twins: a twin fed unflagged hallucinations is worse than none.
shift_bullet: under blur or a phase-contrast input every model's prediction fails, and whether σ warns depends on the training run for all models: ChipStain's σ rises in {{n_shift_cs_defocus_seeds_ok}} seeds (including the released one) but falls in {{n_shift_cs_defocus_seeds_down}}. σ is therefore **not** a reliable drift alarm; added noise, in contrast, is flagged by every model in every seed.
nucleus_bullet: per-nucleus σ flags wrong detections only weakly (AUROC {{n_nuc_cs}}), no better than a dim-nucleus heuristic ({{n_nuc_dim_cs}}); we use it as a review aid, not a filter.
counting_bullet: counting on the prediction reaches nuclei F1 {{n_full_segf1}}; the dataset author's Cellpose model, which segments nuclei directly from bright-field, reaches {{n_cp_f1}}. For counting alone, direct segmentation is better; ChipStain adds a fluorescence-like image and a calibrated σ.
prolif_bullet: label-free counts give population doubling times within {{n_pl_cs_bias_all}} % (mean over seeds) of the real-stain reference; a σ gate fixed on validation data cuts this to {{n_pl_cs_bias_gate}} % (the same gate on the U-Net's TTA disagreement: {{n_pl_bt_bias_all}} → {{n_pl_bt_bias_gate}} % — the gate helps both). On a 60 h, 240-frame recording: {{n_tl_dt_pred}} h vs {{n_tl_dt_real}} h from the real stain.
neural_bullet: on human iPSC-derived motor neurons (dish, not chip) the HeLa model reaches Pearson r {{n_nz_cs_r}} zero-shot (but undercounts nuclei by about half, and its σ stays in the normal range — it does not warn); fine-tuning on one well raises r to {{n_nf_cs_k1_r}} ({{n_nf_cs_k20_r}} with {{n_nf_kmax}} wells; one seed).
ablation_bullet: one factor at a time, 3 seeds each; robust effects: {{n_abl_robust}}.
limitations_short: Validation is on 2-D HeLa cells in one well plate (one imaging session) and neurons in a dish — **no chip data**. ChipStain trades {{n_mae_rel}} % MAE for its uncertainty. Its σ is strongest at ranking pixel errors, calibration and catching catastrophic frames in distribution; under blur or a new modality it warns only in some training runs (as do the baselines), at the nucleus level it is no better than a simple heuristic, and a direct segmenter counts nuclei better. References are automatic StarDist labels. One of three seeds fails on two fields (σ flags them).
impact_short: Once fine-tuned on a few paired images from a device: a quality-controlled, label-free nuclear channel for long OoC recordings — growth and viability curves without dye exposure or fixation, a freed fluorescence channel, and a σ gate that keeps catastrophic frames out of the analysis (in distribution; drift must still be checked with paired images). CPU inference, no proprietary dependencies.

neural_video: On human stem-cell-derived motor neurons, the model transfers partly even without retraining, and fine-tuning on a single well raises the correlation from {{n_nz_cs_r}} to {{n_nf_cs_k1_r}}.
calibration_bullet: ChipStain's σ is approximately calibrated out of the box — the nominal 95 % interval covers {{n_cal_95}} % of test pixels (validation-fitted scale ×{{n_cal_scale}}) — whereas the U-Nets' TTA disagreement needs ×{{n_cal_unet_scale}} rescaling: it can rank, not quantify.
cellpose_pred_text: Replacing our watershed by Cellpose's generic fluorescence nuclei model, F1 on the real stain is {{n_cpp_real}} and on ChipStain's predictions {{n_cpp_pred}} — part of the gap is the segmenter, part is the prediction.
cellpose_shift_text: Under 2 px blur Cellpose's F1 drops from {{n_cps_clean}} to {{n_cps_blur2}} and it returns no uncertainty at all; ChipStain's σ does not reliably warn in that situation either (§6.7), so neither route protects a user against an imaging change.
